one_liner: Julia algebraic multigrid solver for graph-Laplacian systems; 6.6-13.6x faster than PETSc GAMG on social, web and optimization graphs.
what_it_does: Solves L x = b where L is the Laplacian of a connected weighted graph (symmetric, zero row sums, constant null vector) and b has zero mean. It returns the zero-mean solution to relative residual 1e-8 by default. The API is two calls: `h = setup(A)` builds a multilevel hierarchy with no parameters to tune, and `x, info = solve(h, b)` reuses that hierarchy for any number of right-hand sides; `LAMGOptions(tol=..., max_cycles=...)` adjusts stopping. It is a Julia package used from a checkout of the repository and takes a `SparseMatrixCSC`. It is not a general AMG preconditioner like PETSc GAMG: `setup` asserts that its input is a graph Laplacian.
how_it_is_fast: It implements Lean Algebraic Multigrid (Livne and Brandt, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 2012). Exact low-degree elimination, a Schur complement over an independent set of nodes with degree at most 4, alternates with caliber-1 (piecewise-constant) aggregation. Because of this, the Galerkin coarse operators stay as sparse as the graph and do not fill in around scale-free hubs the way classical AMG does. Nodes are grouped into aggregates by the affinity (squared cosine) of K=4 Gauss-Seidel-relaxed test vectors, subject to an energy-ratio guard. LAMG+ adds a strength-of-connection veto and a selective caliber-2 interpolation that fix stalls on grid-aligned anisotropy. The paper credits the low per-edge constants to a self-gated reverse Cuthill-McKee reordering, single-pass Gustavson-fused Schur extraction, allocation-free elimination and an in-place, residual-maintaining Gauss-Seidel kernel.
when_to_use: Laplacian solves on large irregular graphs (social, citation, web, optimization/network-flow), where PETSc GAMG and BoomerAMG slow down by up to an order of magnitude. Class means: 0.47 vs 3.10 us/nnz on social, 0.15 vs 2.04 on optimization.

Finite-element and structural graph Laplacians. Among the robust solvers it was fastest there (for example bmwcra_1 0.08 vs 0.28 us/nnz for approxchol_lap) and leanest in memory (21-30 bytes/nnz vs 33-55 for approximate Cholesky).
Graphs with high mean degree: the paper's rule 'LAMG+ wins iff mean degree >= 30' picked the faster solver against approxChol 91% of the time.
Many right-hand sides on one graph (the hierarchy is reused), or lower-accuracy solves: at 1e-4 its geometric-mean speedup over approxchol_lap rises from 0.99x to 1.20x.
Julia pipelines (spectral clustering, electrical flow, interior-point network flow) that want a solver depending only on Julia standard libraries.
when_not_to_use: Meshes, grids, roads and reservoir models: PETSc GAMG is faster on mesh/grid (0.23 vs 0.84 us/nnz), 3D grid (0.25 vs 1.30), road (0.57 vs 0.68) and SPE (0.90 vs 1.09), and BoomerAMG is faster still on grids.
Social, web, citation and chimera graphs when Laplacians.jl approxchol_lap is an option: it is faster there (social 0.25 vs 0.47, web 0.29 vs 0.37, chimera 0.14 vs 0.40 us/nnz).
C or C++ codebases: the solver is Julia-only and no C API is documented.

General SPD, SDDM or unsymmetric matrices, and disconnected graphs: `setup` asserts zero row sums, and the library handles several components by reducing to one connected component (`largest_component`) instead of solving them all.

Multi-core or distributed runs, and memory-tight web/social workloads. All published timings are single-threaded, the paper calls distributed coarsening unresolved, and the hierarchy takes 62-80 bytes/nnz on web/social graphs vs 32-40 for approxChol.

integration.dependencies: none beyond Julia standard libraries (LinearAlgebra, SparseArrays, Random, Statistics, Printf); the comparison scripts also need Laplacians.jl, HYPRE.jl, PyCall/pyAMG and PETSc_jll in a separate environment
integration.platforms: any platform Julia supports (no other restriction documented); the paper's timings are from an Apple M5 Pro
integration.thread_safety: not documented; published runs are single-threaded (julia -t1), and when nthreads() > 1 the residual and multicolor Gauss-Seidel kernels spread over threads on levels with at least 20,000 nodes

gotchas: The right-hand side must be compatible (zero mean), and the solution is returned orthogonal to the constant vector. The default `max_cycles` is 100, so check `info.cycles` and the residual on hard inputs.
Setup is randomized (relaxed test vectors) but seeded with a fixed MersenneTwister seed (0xfa11), so runs repeat exactly unless you change `LAMGOptions.seed`.

The class-comparison harness defaults to graphs with at most 5,000,000 nonzeros and 6 graphs per class. PETSc GAMG, pyAMG and CMG run in subprocesses (PETSc GAMG from the prebuilt PETSc_jll binary, timed inside the subprocess with startup excluded), and hypre runs through HYPRE.jl, which contradicts the paper's statement that every competitor runs in the same Julia process.
Version 0.1.0 with no release tags. The package UUID is hand-written, and the README installs it from the cloned project, not from a package registry.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick AMGCL (C++ header-only AMG with faster setup than PETSc GAMG) for PDE and mesh systems in C++. Pick apxchol for parallel approximate-Cholesky Laplacian/SDDM solves from C++. Pick LAMG+ for serial Julia work on graph Laplacians, especially FE/structural or high-degree graphs, where it beats approximate Cholesky.
verified_claims_summary: Source: the author's arXiv preprint in the repo (doc/lamg_plus.tex). Setup plus solve to 1e-8 relative residual, run serially on an Apple M5 Pro and reported as mean microseconds per nonzero for each graph class over a class-stratified SuiteSparse/SNAP corpus plus synthetic families. LAMG+ beats PETSc GAMG on social/citation (0.47 vs 3.10), web (0.37 vs 2.76), optimization (0.15 vs 2.04) and the chimera families, ties on FE/structural (0.12), and loses on mesh/grid, 3D grid, road, SPE and star. PETSc, hypre and pyAMG were prebuilt binaries with unstated build flags.
